title: Unveiling the mechanism for enhanced mechanical–electrical–tribological property integration in CuCrZr/Cu laminated metallic composites via cryorolling and short-term annealing
abstract: Abstract CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr laminated metallic composites (LMCs) were fabricated by hot rolling (HR) followed by cryorolling (CR) and subsequent short-term annealing. The CuCrZr layers accounted for 20.0 vol% of the composite, while the core layer consisted of low-cost pure Cu. The resulting LMCs exhibited enhanced ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and wear resistance relative to the constituent materials. Furthermore, the electrical conductivity of the LMCs was significantly higher than that of the initial CuCrZr (38.3%IACS). After annealing at 673 K for 30 min, the LMCs reached a UTS of 292 MPa, an electrical conductivity of 96.7%IACS, and a wear rate of 2.38 × 10 –4  mm 3 ∙N –1 ∙m –1 . These improvements were primarily attributed to optimized precipitation strengthening in the CuCrZr layers and the presence of a high density of annealing twins in the Cu layers. Microstructural characterization revealed uniformly distributed Cr-rich precipitates (≈ 4 nm) in the CuCrZr layer of the CR-A673K sample. Meanwhile, the Cu layer exhibited an annealing-twin area fraction of 43.2% and a 10% increase in the length fraction of Σ3 grain boundaries. This study demonstrates the feasibility of synchronizing CuCrZr aging with Cu recrystallization via CR and short-term annealing, thereby offering a practical design strategy for developing high-performance, low-cost alternatives to pure copper.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Pure copper is widely used in the electrical industry due to its excellent electrical conductivity; however, its relatively low strength and poor wear resistance limit its use in critical connecting components [ 1 ]. About 80% of mechanical component failures worldwide are caused by wear [ 2 ,  3 ], with fretting wear alone responsible for nearly 60% of automotive electrical failures [ 4 ], underscoring the urgent need to develop higher-performance copper-based materials. To address the mechanical limitations of pure copper, researchers have prepared various copper-based composite systems [ 5 ,  6 ]. However, in dissimilar metal composite systems (such as Cu–Al [ 7 ,  8 ] and Cu–Steel [ 9 ]), controlling the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds remains a major challenge [ 10 ]. Consequently, CuCrZr/Cu dissimilar copper alloy composites have attracted increasing interest due to their combination of the high strength of CuCrZr and the excellent electrical conductivity of pure copper [ 11 ,  12 ].

Rolling has been widely implemented in the preparation of layered composite materials [ 13 ,  14 – 15 ]. Cu/CuCrZr composites, fabricated using methods such as accumulative rolling (ARB) [ 11 ] and powder metallurgy combined with rolling [ 12 ], have shown high strength, good ductility, and moderately high electrical conductivity. Nonetheless, several limitations remain: first, achieving substantial performance enhancement typically requires a high volume fraction of CuCrZr, substantially increasing the material cost (the price of pure copper is only 38% of that of CuCrZr [ 16 ]); second, comprehensive research on wear resistance is still insufficient.

From the perspective of engineering applications, developing low-cost and short-process material systems has become an important trend [ 17 ,  18 ]. For layered metal composites, optimizing the thickness ratio is an effective approach to balancing performance and cost [ 19 ]. However, rolling with a large thickness ratio presents challenges due to differences in physical properties and deformation behavior among layers, which result in uneven stress distribution, reduced interface bonding, and even premature fracture [ 20 ,  21 – 22 ]. During ARB processing, plastic-flow instability often emerges earlier in one layer [ 23 ]. Reihanian et al. [ 24 ] investigated necking and fracture in hard layers during ARB and found that a large thickness difference leads to a lower critical strain for necking, thereby increasing deformation instability. Ren et al. [ 25 ] employed the combination of deep learning and crystal plasticity modeling to predict metallic material properties and highlighted the essential role of stress-strain distribution in performance prediction. Therefore, it is necessary to explore new pathways for preparing CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr layered composites with a large thickness ratio that achieve excellent overall performance with lower cost.

Cryorolling (CR) offers a promising solution to these challenges. The CR process can enhance the deformation efficiency of composite materials [ 26 ], improve interface bonding quality [ 27 ], and promote more uniform deformation among layers [ 28 ]. In addition, compared with conventional room-temperature rolling (RTR), the yield strength (YS) and UTS of pure copper processed by CR are significantly improved due to dislocation accumulation [ 29 ]. CR CuCrZr exhibits higher twin density and dislocation density, and its YS, UTS, and uniform elongation surpass those of CuCrZr rolled at room temperature under the same strain conditions [ 30 ]. However, studies focused on fabricating CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr composites with a large thickness ratio via CR, along with systematic analysis of their structure-property correlations, are still limited.

In this study, CR combined with short-time annealing was employed for the first time to successfully prepare CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr layered composites with a large thickness ratio, excellent comprehensive performance, and high economic feasibility. The effects of this processing route on the microstructure and properties were systematically analyzed, the strengthening mechanisms were clarified, and a feasible strategy for developing low-cost, high-performance copper-based composites was proposed.

sections.heading: Experimental
paragraphs: Commercially pure Cu (99.9 wt%) and Cu-0.78Cr-0.13Zr (wt%) alloy sheets with identical dimensions of 60 mm × 30 mm were used as the initial materials. The thicknesses of pure Cu and CuCrZr alloy were 1.6 mm and 0.2 mm, respectively. The Cu sheets were annealed at 723 K for 1 h, whereas the CuCrZr alloy sheets were solution-treated at 1273 K for 10 min followed by water quenching. Figure  1 a illustrates the detailed fabrication procedure of the LMCs. Initially, the contact surfaces of all strips were mechanically cleaned with a wire brush to remove oxides and contaminants. The strips were then stacked in the sequence CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr and secured by steel wire at the four corners. All sheets were oriented parallel to the original rolling direction. During HR, the stacked plates were heated to 873 K before rolling, and each pass was preceded by 5 min of reheating, achieving a total reduction ratio of 50%. Subsequently, CR was applied to obtain a total thickness reduction ratio of 75%, with a reduction of 5% per pass. Before each CR pass, the sheet was immersed in liquid nitrogen, with the initial immersion lasting 20 min and each subsequent immersion lasting 3 min. The CR samples were then annealed at 623 K and 673 K for 30 min, designated as CR-A623K and CR-A673K, respectively. The rolling direction, transverse direction, and normal (thickness) direction were denoted as RD, TD, and ND. Fig. 1 ( a ) Schematic diagram of the preparation route for CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs, and ( b ) macroscopic overview of the as-rolled sheet and corresponding test specimens

Figure  1 b shows the macroscopic overview of the as-rolled LMCs and the corresponding test specimens. The mechanical properties of the CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs were evaluated by hardness testing and tensile testing. Hardness measurements were conducted under a 50 gf load (≈ 490 mN) with a dwell time of 10 s, and five measurements were taken for each sample. Tensile specimens were cut parallel to the RD, with a gauge length of 15 mm and a width of 3 mm. Tensile tests were performed at room temperature at a loading speed of 1 mm∙min –1  and were repeated three times for each condition. The peel test was performed using a universal testing machine at a crosshead speed of 50 mm∙min –1 .
where  L  is the gauge length,  R  is the measured resistance, and  A  is the cross-sectional area of the sample.

Friction and wear tests were performed using a ball-on-disk tribometer with a GCr15 steel ball (6 mm diameter) as the counterbody. The test conditions were as follows: a normal load of 1 N, a rotational speed of 167 r∙min –1 , and a total sliding distance of 500 m. Each condition was tested three times. The 3D surface morphology of the wear tracks was examined using a VHX5000 ultra-deep-field 3D optical microscope. The RD-ND sections, tensile fracture morphology, and wear scar morphology were observed using a TESCAN MIRA3 LMU scanning electron microscope (SEM).

The microstructure of the initial materials and LMCs was characterized using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Samples for EBSD were ground with SiC abrasive papers up to 2000 grit and then polished to a mirror finish using diamond suspensions with particle sizes of 2.5 μm and 0.5 μm, followed by surface treatment with an IM4000 argon ion-beam polisher to remove the deformation layer. EBSD mapping was performed with a step size of 0.2 μm. Collected data were processed and analyzed using Oxford Instruments Aztec Crystal and TSL OIM Analysis software.

The bonding interface and constituent layers of the samples were further examined using a Philips CM200 field-emission gun transmission electron microscope (FEG-TEM) operating at 200 kV. TEM samples of the LMCs were prepared using a Thermo Fisher Scientific Helios G4 PFIB focused-ion-beam system with the RD-ND plane as the observation plane. For TEM analysis of the CuCrZr layer, the composite was thinned until only the CuCrZr remained; a 3 mm disc was then punched and electropolished using a twin-jet system in HNO3:CH3OH (3:7) solution. X-ray diffraction (XRD) (Cu Kα) and Jade software were used to identify the phases in each layer of the composite after CR. Dislocation density was quantified via Modified Williamson–Hall (MWH) analysis. The XRD experimental parameters were as follows: a scanning range of 30°–100° 2 θ , a scanning speed of 2°∙min –1 , and a step size of 0.01°.

sections.heading: Microstructure of CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs
paragraphs: Figure  2  displays the microstructure of the initial materials and the as-fabricated LMCs. After annealing at 723 K for 1 h, pure Cu achieved recrystallization accompanied by grain growth, resulting in an average grain size of 23.43 μm. After solution treatment at 1273 K for 10 min, the CuCrZr alloy exhibited smaller grains than annealed pure Cu, with an average grain size of 17.76 μm. The SEM micrograph of the RD–ND cross-section of the CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr composite after HR and subsequent CR is presented in Fig.  2 c. Microscopic examination confirmed the absence of pores or cracks at the bonding interfaces. Furthermore, the bonding interfaces appear predominantly straight, indicating robust metallurgical bonding. After rolling, the thickness of each CuCrZr layer was 50.3 μm, whereas the pure Cu layer reached 387.8 μm. The post-rolling thickness ratio (CuCrZr: Cu: CuCrZr) remained nearly identical to the initial ratio of 0.2:1.6:0.2. Fig. 2 Microstructures of the ( a ) Cu and ( b ) CuCrZr alloy; ( c ) SEM image of the CR CuCrZr/Cu LMCs

EBSD maps obtained from regions near the bonding interfaces (Fig.  3 ) reveal the microstructural evolution of the constituent Cu and CuCrZr layers under different processing states. In the CR sample, grains in both the Cu and CuCrZr layers exhibit elongated morphologies, and the CuCrZr grains are markedly finer than those in the Cu layer. After annealing, the Cu layer underwent extensive recrystallization accompanied by grain coarsening and annealing twin (AT) development. In contrast, the CuCrZr layer retained its deformed grain structure with negligible changes. Grain orientation spread (GOS) analysis confirms that the CuCrZr layer predominantly comprises deformed grains across all states, with minimal recrystallization. The deformed-grain frequency in the CuCrZr layer remained close to 70% in all three conditions, while the recrystallized fraction never exceeded 10%. The absence of notable recrystallization is attributed to the 673 K annealing temperature being below the recrystallization threshold of the CuCrZr alloy [ 32 ,  33 ]. By contrast, the Cu layer exhibited pronounced structural transformation. Similar to the CuCrZr layer, the Cu layer in the CR state was dominated by deformed grains; however, after annealing, it underwent near-complete recrystallization, with recrystallized grains occupying ~ 99% of the area and deformed grains reduced to ~ 0%. Furthermore, the recrystallized-grain content of the Cu layer after 673 K/30 min annealing increased by 0.71% relative to 623 K/30 min. Fig. 3 IPF and GOS images at the sample interface and the corresponding fractions of recrystallized, sub-structured, and deformed grains in the Cu layer: (a 1 –a 3 ) CR; (b 1 –b 3 ) CR-A623K; (c 1 –c 3 ) CR-A673K

Figure  4  presents the grain boundary maps and misorientation-angle distribution histograms for the Cu and CuCrZr layers in each processing state. The evolution of misorientation characteristics was quantified by the fractions of low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs, θ < 15°) and high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs, θ ≥ 15°). In the CR samples, both constituent layers exhibited high LAGB fractions, which are typical of severe plastic deformation where dislocation accumulation promotes LAGB formation [ 34 ,  35 ]. The LAGB fraction in the CuCrZr layer (76.4%) of the CR state was higher than that in the Cu layer (68.8%). After annealing, the LAGB/HAGB fractions in the CuCrZr layer showed negligible variation, remaining stable at 78.0%/22.0% (CR-A623K) and 77.9%/22.1% (CR-A673K). In contrast, the Cu layer exhibited a substantial LAGB-to-HAGB conversion owing to recrystallization, with the HAGB fraction increasing from 31.2% (CR) to 97.1% (CR-A623K) and further to 97.6% (CR-A673K). Fig. 4 Grain boundary maps and misorientation-angle distribution histograms of the constituent layers: (a 1 –a 3 ) CR; (b 1 –b 3 ) CR-A623K; (c 1 –c 3 ) CR-A673K

Figure  5  displays TEM images of the CuCrZr/Cu interface after rolling, along with the microstructures in the CuCrZr layer of the CR, CR-A623K, and CR-A673K samples. Figure  5 a shows the interface morphology and adjacent grain structure after HR and CR processing. A continuous and well-bonded interface is visible between the CuCrZr and Cu layers, and the CuCrZr layer exhibits significantly finer grains than the Cu layer. Figure  5 b reveals nanoscale deformation twins (DTs) within the CuCrZr layer, confirmed by the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern showing distinct diffraction spots. Similar observations have been reported in studies of CR-processed CuCrZr [ 36 ,  37 ]. Furthermore, a high density of dislocations was observed adjacent to the DTs. The presence of twin boundaries serves as barriers to dislocation motion, thereby strengthening the matrix. In both annealed samples, distinct precipitates were observed, with the CR-A673K sample exhibiting a higher density of precipitates than the CR-A623K sample. Fig. 5 TEM images of ( a ) the CuCrZr/Cu interface after rolling and the CuCrZr layer in ( b ) CR, ( c ) CR-A623K, and ( d ) CR-A673K

XRD analysis was performed on the CuCrZr layer of each sample to identify the phase constituents. Figure  6 a displays only the characteristic FCC Cu reflections, with no visible additional peaks. Because the starting alloy contained a low Cr content and underwent solution treatment before rolling, the Cr-related diffraction peaks were too weak to appear distinctly in the overall spectrum. This phenomenon is consistent with previous reports on CuCrZr alloys [ 38 ,  39 ]. In FCC metals, the crystal plane with the highest atomic packing density is the (111) plane, which also serves as the primary slip plane. However, the XRD patterns of the CR and annealed samples display an unusually weak Cu(111) peak, indicating that the grains were heavily deformed. Following severe plastic deformation, progressive grain refinement leads to extensive slip activity; dislocation accumulation on the primary slip plane obstructs further slip, thereby activating secondary slip systems [ 40 ]. Additionally, after CR, the strongest peak in the Cu layer appears on the (220) plane, while the CuCrZr layer exhibits its strongest peak on the (200) plane, reflecting crystallographic texture evolution. After magnifying and fitting the XRD spectra in the 2θ range of 44.2–44.7° (Fig.  6 b), peaks corresponding to the Cr phase and the Cu 8 Zr 3  phase were detected. In the CR-A623K and CR-A673K samples, the intensities of these peaks increased significantly and reached their highest intensity in the CR-A673K sample. In addition, the peak positions of both the Cr and Cu 8 Zr 3  phases shifted toward higher angles, indicating a progressive increase in precipitation in the CuCrZr layer of the CR-A673K sample. Fig. 6 ( a ) XRD patterns of the CuCrZr layer in each sample; ( b ) magnified XRD peaks of Cr and Cu 8 Zr 3

Table  1  summarizes the calculated dislocation densities of the CuCrZr layer under different conditions. For the CR sample, the dislocation density reached 1.4 × 10 15  m –2 . During annealing, dislocation recovery occurred, reducing the density to 9.9 × 10 14  m –2  (CR-A623K) and 9.5 × 10 14  m –2  (CR-A673K). Table 1 Dislocation density of the CuCrZr layer under different conditions Conditions Dislocation density ρ, (m –2 ) CR 1.4 × 10 15 CR-A623K 9.9 × 10 14 CR-A673K 9.5 × 10 14

sections.heading: Mechanical properties of CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs
paragraphs: Figure  7 a presents the microhardness values of each layer of the CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs under different conditions. The low initial hardness of Cu (56.1 HV) and CuCrZr (64.6 HV) resulted from their respective annealing and solution treatments. The secondary phases present in CuCrZr, arising from the limited solubility of Cr and Zr within the Cu matrix, contribute to its slightly higher hardness compared with pure Cu. In composites comprising different materials, the microhardness of individual layers often differs after rolling [ 45 ,  46 ]. After rolling, the hardness of both layers increased substantially; the CuCrZr layer reached 171.8 HV, significantly higher than the 106.3 HV of the Cu layer. This hardness increase was mainly due to work hardening driven by the sharp rise in dislocation density during deformation. CuCrZr exhibits a stronger work-hardening capability than pure Cu. After annealing at 623 K for 30 min and 673 K for 30 min, the hardness of the Cu layer decreased to nearly its initial level, whereas the hardness of the CuCrZr layer showed a slight increase after 673 K/30 min (188.4 HV). Fig. 7 CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs under different conditions: ( a ) hardness of each layer; ( b ) engineering stress-strain curves; ( c ) mechanical performance statistics; ( d ) work-hardening rate

Based on the engineering stress-strain curves, the UTS values of the initial Cu and CuCrZr sheets were 225 MPa and 230 MPa, respectively. The corresponding YS values were 55 MPa for Cu and 92 MPa for CuCrZr. After rolling, the UTS of the CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs increased to 427 MPa. Following annealing at 623 K and 673 K, the composite retained UTS values of 280 MPa and 292 MPa, respectively. The YS increased to 178 MPa for CR-A623K and 190 MPa for CR-A673K. Notably, the CR-A673K sample exhibited both a higher uniform elongation and a higher UTS than the CR-A623K sample. Compared with the initial CuCrZr, the CR-A673K sample sacrificed only 2.4% of uniform elongation while achieving a 27% increase in UTS and a 129% increase in YS. Moreover, compared with the initial CuCrZr, the CR-A673K sample only sacrificed 2.4% in uniform elongation (UE), achieving an increase of 27% in UTS and 129% in YS, respectively. Similar significant performance improvements are also found in other composite materials featuring microstructures of alternating soft and hard layers [ 47 ,  48 ,  49 – 50 ]. This exceptional property combination in CR-A673K arises from the coupled effects of recrystallization in the Cu layer and precipitation strengthening in the CuCrZr layer, as corroborated by the layer-specific microhardness data. For the Cu layer, 623 K already exceeds the recrystallization temperature of Cu.

Figure  7 d presents the work-hardening rate curve derived from the true stress-strain curve. Among all samples, the initial sample showed the highest work-hardening rate, followed by the annealed LMCs. The higher work-hardening rates in the annealed samples relative to the as-rolled state indicate an improved ability to delay necking onset, thereby enhancing the uniform elongation of the LMCs.

Figure  8  illustrates the fracture morphology of tensile specimens in different states. After tensile deformation, all specimens exhibited varying degrees of interfacial delamination caused by pronounced property mismatches between the Cu and CuCrZr layers in the CR, CR-A623K, and CR-A673K samples, resulting in deformation incompatibility during tension. The Cu layers underwent pronounced necking, whereas the CuCrZr layers exhibited limited necking, indicating that most plastic deformation was accommodated by the Cu layers. As high-temperature treatment promotes elemental diffusion and improves interfacial bonding effectiveness [ 51 ], a broader well-bonded region was observed on the TD–ND surface of the fracture in the CR-A673K sample (Fig.  8 c 2 ). Fracture surfaces of both layers displayed ductile dimples; these dimples were significantly larger and deeper in the Cu layers than in the CuCrZr layers. The Cu layers exhibited a bimodal dimple size distribution, whereas the CuCrZr layers contained uniformly fine, shallow dimples. These observations are consistent with the fracture morphology on the RD–ND plane (Fig.  8 a 1 , b 1 , c 1 ) and confirm the superior plastic deformation capacity of the Cu layers. Furthermore, as annealing temperature increased, the dimples in the Cu layers became significantly larger and deeper, while the CuCrZr layer showed minimal change. This coarsening of dimples correlates directly with recrystallization in the Cu layers (Fig.  3 a). Fig. 8 Tensile fracture morphology of different samples: (a 1 –a 4 ) CR; (b 1 –b 4 ) CR-A623K; (c 1 –c 4 ) CR-A673K

The interfacial bonding quality is a critical property of the composite [ 52 ,  53 ]. Figure  9  presents the peel strength of the CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs. The CR samples exhibited the lowest bonding strength, with an average peel strength of 2.96 N/mm. After annealing, bonding strength increased significantly. The CR-A623K samples reached an average of 4.73 N/mm, corresponding to a 59.8% improvement relative to the CR condition. Upon further temperature elevation, the CR-A673K samples achieved a peel strength of 6.49 N/mm, representing a 119% increase compared with the CR state. Elevated temperature accelerates elemental diffusion, thereby enhancing the bonding strength [ 54 ]. Fig. 9 Peel strength of CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs

sections.heading: Electrical conductivity of CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs
paragraphs: Figure  10  shows the electrical conductivity of all samples. After solution treatment, the electrical conductivity of CuCrZr was 38.3%IACS. Despite incorporating solution-treated CuCrZr, the as-rolled LMC retained 90.5%IACS. After annealing at 673 K, conductivity increased to 96.7%IACS. The CR-A623K sample exhibited intermediate conductivity (94.8%IACS). As evidenced by Fig.  7 , CR-A673K achieved 96.7%IACS while maintaining superior mechanical properties. Fig. 10 Electrical conductivity under different conditions

sections.heading: Friction and wear performance of CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs
paragraphs: Figure  11  presents the friction curves, average friction coefficients, and wear rates of the investigated samples. The friction curves (Fig.  11 a) indicated stable friction behavior at CR, CR-A623K, and CR-A673K, with lower coefficient variability than monolithic Cu and CuCrZr. This stability arises from their friction coefficients stabilizing near a constant value after a brief run-in period [ 55 ,  56 ]. The average friction coefficients of all the samples were within the range of 0.54–0.65 (Fig.  11 b). Figure  10 c compares the wear rates of all the samples. The Cu sample exhibited the highest wear rate (6.73 × 10 –4  mm 3 ·N –1 ·m –1 ), whereas the CR-A673K sample presented the lowest (2.38 × 10 –4  mm 3 ·N –1 ·m –1 ). Fig. 11 Friction and wear performance of different samples: ( a ) friction curve; ( b ) average friction coefficient; ( c ) wear rate

Figure  12  shows SEM images of the worn surfaces. As shown in Fig.  12 a, the worn surface of the initial Cu exhibited extensive peeling, shallow grooves, and debris from adhesion, indicating a mixed wear mechanism dominated by fatigue wear and adhesive wear, with abrasive wear as a secondary mechanism. Deep and uneven wear pits were also observed, and the wear edges appeared irregular along the sliding direction, consistent with its high wear rate (6.73 × 10 –4  mm 3 ∙N –1 ∙m –1 ). For the initial CuCrZr (Fig.  12 b), the worn surface exhibited a large number of grooves with minor delamination and adhered debris. The primary wear mechanism was abrasive wear, accompanied by secondary adhesive wear and delamination. Figure  12 c shows that the worn surface of the CR sample exhibited extensive shallow plow grooves and loose debris without deep cuts, reflecting a mixed abrasive-adhesive wear mechanism with comparable contributions from both mechanisms. The wear-track width of the CR sample was clearly narrower than those of the initial materials, in agreement with the improved wear resistance shown in Fig.  11 c. The heat-treated samples also exhibited a mixed abrasive-adhesive wear mechanism; however, the proportion of abrasive wear was significantly higher. Moreover, the plow grooves in the CR-A673K sample were considerably shallower than those in CR-A623K. The CR-A673K sample exhibited the smallest wear footprint. Fig. 12 SEM images of worn sample surfaces: ( a ) Cu; ( b ) CuCrZr; ( c ) CR; ( d ) CR-A623K; ( e ) CR-A673K

In addition to the wear morphology of the specimen surfaces, the counterpart (friction-pair) surfaces were also examined. Figure  13  illustrates the surface morphology of the counterparts corresponding to the different specimens. The Cu and CuCrZr samples, as the initial materials, produced the largest wear areas on their respective counterparts. Among them, CuCrZr generated the maximum wear area (396946 µm 2 ). However, the friction-pair surface of the Cu sample exhibited a larger quantity of adhered lamellar debris, whereas the CuCrZr sample produced a smaller quantity of finer debris particles. This observation correlates with the dominant wear mechanisms: the Cu sample primarily underwent fatigue wear and adhesive wear, while the CuCrZr sample predominantly exhibited abrasive wear. Similarly, the CR sample also showed adhesive wear as a significant mechanism, with adhered debris observed on the counterpart surface. The debris size of the CR sample was intermediate between those of the Cu and CuCrZr samples. Moreover, the wear area of the CR counterpart was significantly smaller than that of the initial materials. The LMCs exhibited improved wear resistance following annealing. SEM analysis revealed no adhered debris on the counterpart surfaces of the CR-A623K and CR-A673K samples. Additionally, the wear area of the CR-A673K counterpart was the smallest, consistent with the wear rate data shown in Fig.  11 c. Fig. 13 Wear surfaces of friction pairs for each sample

To further compare differences in wear characteristics, an ultra-deep-field microscope was used to characterize the wear profiles and quantify both width and depth (Fig.  14 ). The wear-trace profiles further confirmed the enhanced wear resistance achieved through material strengthening. The sample surfaces were subjected to plowing by the GCr15 steel counterbody, resulting in the accumulation of displaced material along both sides of the wear tracks, forming ridge-like asperities. The Cu sample exhibited the largest wear track, with a width of 663 μm and a depth of ~ 18.19 μm. Although the CuCrZr sample exhibited comparable hardness, its wear-track width and depth were reduced to 644 μm and ~ 15.59 μm, respectively; however, its wear rate remained relatively high at 4.44 × 10 –4  mm 3 ∙N –1 ∙m –1 . In contrast, the annealed LMCs exhibited 65–75% lower wear depths compared with the initial materials. The CR-A673K sample displayed the shallowest and narrowest wear trace (width 375 μm, depth ~ 4.65 μm), representing a 43% reduction in width and a 74% reduction in depth relative to the initial CuCrZr sample. These findings demonstrate a clear positive correlation between hardness and wear resistance, with the CR-A673K sample—having the highest hardness—exhibiting the strongest wear resistance. Fig. 14 ( a ) Wear morphology; ( b ) wear width and depth of different samples

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: In this study, CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs were fabricated using a large thickness ratio (0.2:1.6:0.2) to minimize alloy consumption. Few reports have documented the preparation of LMCs with such a high thickness ratio, and no previous studies have described CuCrZr/Cu LMCs containing ≤ 20 vol% CuCrZr (Fig.  15 ). From an economic standpoint, assuming raw material costs of 120 RMB∙kg –1  for CuCrZr [ 16 ] and 46 RMB∙kg –1  for Cu [ 17 ], the calculated raw material cost of the CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs produced in this work was 60.8 RMB∙kg –1 . The cost-performance ratio was defined as UTS × electrical conductivity/material cost (excluding processing losses and manufacturing expenses). The cost-performance ratio of the CR-A673K sample reached ~ 471 (MPa∙%IACS)/RMB, approaching the value for pure Cu (504 (MPa∙%IACS)/RMB) and far exceeding that of the CuCrZr alloy (73 (MPa∙%IACS)/RMB). Additionally, after annealing, the CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs achieved a synergistic enhancement of mechanical, electrical, and tribological properties (UTS 292 MPa, electrical conductivity 96.7%IACS, wear rate 2.38 × 10 –4  mm 3 ·N –1 ·m –1 ). Fig. 15 Performance comparison with other dissimilar copper alloy composites [ 11 ,  12 ,  57 ,  58 ,  59 ,  60 ,  61 – 62 ]

sections.heading: Mechanisms for enhanced mechanical properties
paragraphs: For most single-component metallic materials, increasing annealing temperature typically decreases strength while improving ductility. However, in this study, the material annealed at 673 K for 30 min achieved both higher UTS and greater uniform elongation than the material annealed at 623 K. This anomalous behavior originates from the dual-layer architecture. Distinct layer-specific responses occurred during annealing: recrystallization dominated in the Cu layers, while precipitation strengthening initiated in CuCrZr at 673 K (as shown in Figs.  3  and  7 ). EBSD analysis (Fig.  3 b 3  and Fig.  3 c3) confirmed that the recrystallized-grain fractions in the Cu layers were comparable (98.17% and 98.88%) after annealing at 623 K and 673 K, resulting in nearly identical hardness. However, the CuCrZr layer exhibited higher hardness after 673 K annealing. This difference was related to the number and mean size of precipitates. Annealing at 673 K, which lies within the optimal precipitation range for CuCrZr [ 11 ], promoted precipitation, producing a higher density of Cr-rich particles in the CR-A673K sample than in the CR-A623K sample (Fig.  5 c and d).

Figure  16  compares the precipitate distributions in the CR-A623K and CR-A673K samples using higher-magnification TEM images. For each sample, precipitate sizes were quantified from three randomly acquired TEM micrographs using Gatan DigitalMicrograph™. In the CR-A623K sample, precipitates were primarily distributed in the range of 2–4 nm, whereas the CR-A673K sample contained a greater proportion of precipitates larger than 4 nm. The average precipitate sizes were 3.1 ± 0.9 nm for CR-A623K and 4.0 ± 0.8 nm for CR-A673K. High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) and fast Fourier transform (FFT) confirmed that these nanoscale precipitates were fcc Cr-rich phases. These uniformly dispersed precipitates effectively impeded dislocation motion, increasing the strength of the CuCrZr layer. Consequently, the higher hardness of the CuCrZr layer in the CR-A673K sample contributed to its superior UTS compared with the CR-A623K sample. Fig. 16 High-magnification TEM micrographs showing precipitate distributions with inset size histograms; HRTEM images with corresponding FFT patterns inset: ( a ,  b ) CR-A623K, ( c ,  d ) CR-A673K

Following quantitative analysis, the strength contributions of each layer were obtained (Fig.  17 ). The Cu-layer contributions in CR-A623K and CR-A673K were nearly identical, whereas the precipitation-strengthening contribution in the CuCrZr layer of CR-A673K was markedly higher than in CR-A623K. Fig. 17 Quantitative analysis of strength contributions from each constituent layer

After annealing, the Cu layer contributed predominantly to composite plasticity. Numerous studies have shown that a high content of “special” boundaries enhances ductility, corrosion resistance, fracture toughness, and related properties [ 70 ,  71 ]. In Cu—a low stacking-fault-energy metal—annealing twins (ATs) form once the recrystallization temperature is reached. These twin structures modify boundary energy and mobility, thereby improving mechanical performance by storing dislocations. EBSD quantified the twin area fraction and the length fractions of Σ3 and Σ9 boundaries (Fig.  18 ), with statistics summarized in Fig.  19 . The Cu layer in CR-A673K showed twin area fraction and Σ3/Σ9 length fractions that were higher by 2.6%, 10%, and 1%, respectively, than those in CR-A623K. The proportion of Σ3 boundaries exceeded that of Σ9 boundaries. Moreover, as shown in Fig.  18 a and c, the fraction of twin-free regions (white) was larger in the Cu layer of CR-A623K than in CR-A673K. Compared with random boundaries, Σ3 twins provide superior strain compatibility across interfaces, lowering the likelihood of localized stress concentrations [ 72 ]. Σ3 twins influence both electrical conductivity and plasticity; accordingly, CR-A673K exhibited greater plasticity than CR-A623K. Fig. 18 Twins and twin boundaries in the Cu layer after annealing: ( a - b ) CR-A623K; ( c - d ) CR-A673K Fig. 19 Twin area fraction ( a ) and length fractions of Σ3 and Σ9 boundaries ( b ) in the Cu layer under different annealing conditions

Overall, the excellent mechanical properties of the composite are attributed to the balance between the recrystallization of the Cu layer and the aging of the CuCrZr layer. In the CR-A673K sample, recrystallization occurred in the Cu layer, and the microhardness rapidly decreased to the pre-rolling level; however, abundant annealing twins were present. According to the Smith-Zener pinning effect [ 73 ], the CuCrZr layer forms well-dispersed nanoprecipitates that act as potent obstacles to dislocation slip, thereby significantly strengthening the CuCrZr layer. In addition, at the microscopic level, the composite material is a heterogeneous structure consisting of coarse-grained Cu and fine-grained CuCrZr. You et al. [ 11 ] also prepared dual-heterogeneous-laminated (DHL) Cu/Cu-Cr-Zr composites with alternating coarse-grained Cu and fine-grained CuCrZr layers via annealing. The microscopic mechanism of its deformation with increasing tensile strain was explored. The results show that the significant microstructure heterogeneity in grain size, precipitation distribution, and composition between the Cu and Cu-Cr-Zr layers renders them mechanically incompatible at the layer interface during deformation. The constraint of the CuCrZr layer on the Cu layer induces strain gradients, which are accommodated by the generation of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) [ 74 ]. The generated GNDs accumulate near the interface, giving rise to long-range internal stress, which is referred to as back-stress [ 75 ]. The development of back-stress can enhance the overall strength of the DHL Cu/Cu-Cr-Zr composites. Therefore, the CR-A673K sample exhibits excellent mechanical properties.

sections.heading: Mechanisms for high electrical conductivity
paragraphs: The detailed values of the individual contributions to electrical resistivity (grain boundary, dislocation, precipitation, and solute atoms) were calculated, as shown in Fig.  20 . A comparison revealed that the grain-boundary and dislocation resistivity contributions were comparable in both samples. The primary difference in conductivity between CR-A623K and CR-A673K therefore originated from differences in precipitation resistivity and solute-atom resistivity. In the CR-A623K sample, the solute-atom resistivity constituted the largest portion, reaching 35.5 × 10 –10  Ω·m. In the CR-A673K sample, although solute atoms still contributed most significantly, their concentration was markedly reduced due to enhanced precipitation of Cr and Zr during annealing. As a result, the solute-atom resistivity in CR-A673K dropped to 17.2 × 10 –10  Ω·m. This reduction in solute-atom resistivity accounted for the higher electrical conductivity of the CR-A673K sample relative to CR-A623K. Fig. 20 Contributions of grain boundaries, dislocations, precipitates, and solute atoms to the electrical resistivity in the CuCrZr layers

sections.heading: Mechanisms for high wear resistance
paragraphs: This research, however, is subject to several limitations. While this study successfully demonstrates the feasibility of fabricating composites with a significantly large thickness ratio via CR, the ultimate limit of this ratio has not been fully explored. Due to equipment constraints, even larger thickness ratios could potentially be attempted to determine the critical point at which interface bonding quality or deformation uniformity begins to degrade. Investigating this boundary would provide valuable insights for future industrial scale-up.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In this work, CuCrZr/Cu/CuCrZr LMCs with a high thickness ratio were fabricated by HR and CR followed by short-term annealing. The influence of processing routes on the microstructure and properties of the LMCs was systematically elucidated. The main conclusions are as follows:

(1) After annealing at 673 K, the LMCs exhibited a UTS of 292 MPa and a UE of 18.7%. Compared with the initial CuCrZr alloy, the UE remained essentially unchanged, while the UTS increased by 27%. This enhancement resulted from a dual mechanism: nanoscale Cr-rich precipitation in the CuCrZr layer provided high strength, while abundant annealing twins in the Cu layer preserved ductility.

(2) The CR-A673K sample reached a conductivity of 96.7%IACS, approaching that of pure Cu (100%IACS). This high conductivity stemmed from reduced electron scattering due to solute depletion in the CuCrZr layer and a high fraction (45.5%) of Σ3 grain boundaries with low scattering propensity in the Cu layer.

(3) The CR-A673K sample exhibited the lowest wear rate of 2.38 × 10 –4  mm 3 ∙N –1 ∙m –1 . The improved wear resistance arose from uniformly distributed Cr-rich precipitates (~ 4 nm) in the CuCrZr layer, which enhanced hardness and thereby reduced wear.
